clinical_knowledge.topic: Giant Cell Arteritis with Polymyalgia Rheumatica evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Giant Cell Arteritis with Polymyalgia Rheumatica is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Giant Cell Arteritis with Polymyalgia Rheumatica, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: new severe temple headache, jaw pain when chewing, and transient vision darkening
Key HPI features: 73M presenting with right temporal headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, amaurosis fugax, and ESR 98 mm/hr requiring immediate high-dose prednisone before biopsy.
Objective/Exam findings: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Giant Cell Arteritis with Polymyalgia Rheumatica.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Giant Cell Arteritis with Polymyalgia Rheumatica.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Trigeminal neuralgia without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Any vision changes (amaurosis fugax) — treat immediately with steroids to prevent permanent blindness.
management_principles: Visual symptoms or suspected ischemia require same-day emergency assessment by ophthalmology/rheumatology; the treating clinician should begin urgent glucocorticoid treatment without waiting for confirmatory testing when GCA is strongly suspected.
Arrange temporal-artery ultrasound and/or biopsy promptly, plus ESR/CRP, CBC, metabolic profile, and assessment for aortic involvement; testing should not delay emergency care for threatened vision.
Monitor glucocorticoid adverse effects (glucose, blood pressure, bone protection, infection risk) and use steroid-sparing therapy only under specialist direction.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Giant Cell Arteritis with Polymyalgia Rheumatica: new severe temple headache, jaw pain when chewing, and transient vision darkening. 73M presenting with right temporal headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, amaurosis fugax, and ESR 98 mm/hr requiring immediate high-dose prednisone before biopsy.
reference_soap.objective: Document visual acuity and fields, pupils, full neurologic examination, temporal-artery tenderness/pulse, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, and vital signs. ESR is 98 mm/hr; obtain CRP, CBC/platelets, metabolic profile, and urgent vascular/temporal-artery imaging or biopsy as locally available.
reference_soap.assessment: High suspicion for giant cell arteritis with transient visual ischemia; this is an ophthalmologic emergency with risk of permanent blindness.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Send immediately for emergency ophthalmology/rheumatology evaluation. 2. A treating clinician should start urgent glucocorticoid therapy when suspicion is high; do not wait for biopsy or ultrasound if vision is threatened. 3. Confirm diagnosis promptly and monitor treatment toxicity, blood pressure, glucose, bone protection, and infection risk.

teaching.diagnosis: Giant Cell Arteritis with Polymyalgia Rheumatica
teaching.one_liner: Inflammation of medium and large arteries — most dangerously the temporal artery — causing headache, jaw pain when chewing, and transient vision loss; an ophthalmologic emergency treated with high-dose steroids before biopsy confirmation.
red_flags: Any vision changes (amaurosis fugax) — treat immediately with steroids to prevent permanent blindness

must_ask.say: Where exactly is the headache, and is it new for you?
Does your jaw hurt or get tired when you chew?
Have you had any episodes of vision going dark or blurry?
Is your scalp tender to touch, like when you brush your hair?
Have you had stiffness or aching in your shoulders and hips?
